SeaweedFS.fsync_policy: weed mount's Fsync flushes the client's dirty pages to the co-located volume server (HTTP PUT over loopback) and commits filer metadata over gRPC; it does not fsync the volume .dat or the filer store, so it is NOT a durable per-record barrier (see not_comparable).

differences: FUSE userspace library: OrFS-GO and SeaweedFS both use hanwen/go-fuse/v2; OrFS-Rust uses the fuser crate. All three speak classical /dev/fuse with one request per operation, but they are independent daemons.
Transport shape differs: Go serves its default f0 multi-reader loop; Rust serves its classical fuse transport; SeaweedFS serves go-fuse. Same wire protocol, different daemon concurrency shapes.

Backing I/O: the Go daemon writes synchronously (pwrite/pread); Rust was pinned to --backing-io sync to match, because its default on this host is io_uring; SeaweedFS's FUSE client PUTs data over loopback HTTP to a co-located volume server that writes its own .dat files.
Durability is equal for the OrFS pair (both take one fsync per 4 KiB record) but NOT for SeaweedFS, whose Fsync is a flush-to-co-located-server, not a stable-storage barrier. See not_comparable.
OrFS-GO and OrFS-Rust are both mounted --direct-io (FOPEN_DIRECT_IO); weed mount exposes no such knob. Recorded, not removed.
All three use the same segment/record geometry and the same seeded 4 KiB record payload; the read file is the same size and the same deterministic content.

Container caps are shared (the same container enforces them for all mounts), so no system can be given different resources. The systems' arms run strictly sequentially and a finished system's daemon and volume are released before the next system's arms, so no two systems compete for the shared memory cap.

Within each system the read arms run before the append arms, on a quiet volume: the OrFS append arms retain unbounded history (non-withdrawal), so measuring appends first would evict the read file from the backing page cache and make every --direct-io read a backing I/O. All three systems are measured in the same order.
Host-level variance (page cache state, kernel scheduler, backing device write cache) is not controlled beyond the shared container: run-to-run variance is expected and unquantified here.

not_comparable.reason: The driver issues write(2)+fsync(2) per 4 KiB record on every system, but the systems do not honour it equally. OrFS-GO and OrFS-Rust implement fsync as a durable barrier (one fsync of the authoritative log per record). SeaweedFS 3.99's FUSE client implements Fsync as weed/mount/weedfs_file_sync.go: Fsync -> doFlush -> dirtyPages.FlushData, i.e. an HTTP PUT of the client's dirty pages to the co-located volume server plus a gRPC filer CreateEntry; it performs no fsync of the volume .dat file or the filer store, so it offers no documented per-record durability barrier. The SeaweedFS append rate is therefore NOT equal-durability with the OrFS rows and must not be read as such.

SeaweedFS is a client/server filesystem: even co-located, the FUSE client's data crosses the loopback network stack to the volume server (HTTP) and its metadata crosses gRPC to the filer, unlike the local in-process OrFS daemons. Its read path also serves warm reads from the client's in-process chunk cache, so a warm read never leaves the client process.

The identical pread workload produced a very different shape for SeaweedFS: its 4 KiB random reads ran ~2k IOPS while its 64 KiB random reads ran ~0.3-1.3M IOPS (a ~100-600x gap), and a preceding warm 64 KiB pass did not change the 4 KiB rate (checked directly). The rows are published as measured; they are comparable as syscalls, but SeaweedFS's FUSE client serves some read sizes from an in-process chunk cache and others with a backing round trip, which is not the same data path as the OrFS daemons.

OrFS-GO and OrFS-Rust are both mounted --direct-io (FOPEN_DIRECT_IO); weed mount exposes no direct-I/O knob, so the direct-I/O parity the OrFS pair shares is unavailable for SeaweedFS. Recorded as a caveat rather than silently differing.

The shared 2 GiB cap holds one OrFS daemon plus the driver, but must hold SeaweedFS's whole stack (server + FUSE client) plus the same driver. At SeaweedFS's default Go GC settings its client heap grew past the cap and the kernel OOM-killed the volume server mid-arm on an earlier run. The SeaweedFS processes are therefore run under GOGC=50 GOMEMLIMIT=700MiB; this is an environment-fit knob applied to SeaweedFS only and is recorded, not hidden.

comparability.note: Three mounted storage systems driven by the same shared driver on the same machine and the same device: OrFS-GO, OrFS-Rust, and SeaweedFS's FUSE client. Durability is equal for the OrFS pair (one fsync per 4 KiB record) but not for SeaweedFS, whose Fsync is a flush-to-server, not a stable-storage barrier (see not_comparable) — its append rows are published but must not be read as equal-durability. The systems' arms run strictly sequentially and a finished system's daemon and volume are released before the next system's arms, so no two compete for the shared memory cap (this changes no measured arm). Differences above are the comparability caveats; no row is a ranking. A system that could not be run the same way is recorded as an asymmetry or a named SKIPPED, never a parity claim. The arms block names every coordinate that is missing for a system that mounted; a system that did not mount reports measured=false with its status.

notes: Every row is one bounded arm of the shared driver (cmd/orfscompare) against a mounted filesystem on this machine.

Read the comparability block before comparing any two rows; a row that could not run the same way is recorded as a caveat, not a pass or a parity claim. not_comparable lists the axes that must not be ranked.
The receipt deliberately carries no ranking: two rows are comparable only at the same {workload, writers, readers, block_size} and under the listed configuration differences.
